pos: n. (Jan Amos Komensky, 1592–1670, last bishop of the Unity of the Brethren and father of modern education)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, and Amots, strong; Komensky, of Komna in Moravia.
biblical_def: John Amos Comenius was the last bishop of the old Unity of the Brethren and the most influential educator Europe produced before the nineteenth century. Orphaned young, trained at Herborn and Heidelberg, he was pastor at Fulnek when the White Mountain destroyed Bohemian Protestantism; his library and manuscripts were burned, his wife and two children died in the plague of the flight, and he spent the remaining fifty years in exile at Leszno in Poland, in England, Sweden, Hungary and at last Amsterdam. Out of that he wrote. The Great Didactic and the Janua Linguarum Reserata established teaching by things rather than by rote, by the native tongue before Latin, in graded stages suited to the child, for girls as well as boys and for the poor as well as the rich; the Orbis Pictus of 1658 was the first illustrated schoolbook. Beneath the pedagogy lay a theology: all learning is the knowledge of God's works, and the child is to be led, not driven. His devotional Labyrinth of the World and the Paradise of the Heart is a classic of Czech literature. “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4) was his own question, answered by fifty years of work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines education as the bringing up of a child, and didactic as adapted to teach, preceptive.
webster_full: EDUCA'TION, n. The bringing up, as of a child; instruction; formation of manners.
DIDAC'TIC, a. Adapted to teach; preceptive; containing doctrines, precepts or rules.
EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country.

corruption_summary: The exiled Moravian bishop who gave Europe graded, vernacular, illustrated schooling.
corruption_paragraphs: Comenius is now claimed as a secular founder of pedagogy, with the theology treated as the period packaging around a modern method. The opposite is nearer the truth. He taught by things and in the mother tongue because he believed the creation is God's book and the child God's image; he taught the poor and the girls because he believed every image-bearer is made to know.

The principle to recover is that instruction is a work of patience directed at a person, not a process applied to a unit: “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6), and “Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me” (Mat 19:14). His aim for the nations was Isaiah's — “the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea” (Isa 11:9).

pos: n. (Peter Melius Juhasz, c. 1532–1572, bishop of Debrecen, organiser of the Hungarian Reformed Church)
etymology: Greek Petros, a rock; Hungarian Juhasz, a shepherd, latinised Melius.
biblical_def: Peter Melius was the organiser of the Reformed Church in Hungary and for fourteen years bishop of Debrecen, the city which became and remains its capital. Trained at Wittenberg, he returned convinced on the Reformed rather than the Lutheran side of the sacramental question, and set about giving the Hungarian churches a confession, a government and a defence. He presided over a succession of synods — Tarcal, Torda, Debrecen — which adopted the Second Helvetic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism, established presbyterial oversight under superintendents, and settled the order of worship. His hardest fight was against the antitrinitarians: Francis David, once his ally, carried the Transylvanian church into Unitarianism, and Melius met him in the great public disputations of 1566 and 1568 before King John Sigismund, contending for the deity of Christ and the Trinity from Scripture alone. He published over forty works in Hungarian, including a catechism, confessions, and part of a Bible translation, and he died at Debrecen in 1572 worn out at forty. “I and my Father are one” (Joh 10:30) was the text the disputations turned on.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the Trinity as the union of three persons in one Godhead, and a superintendent as one who has the oversight and charge of something.
webster_full: TRIN'ITY, n. The union of three persons in one Godhead.
SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
DISPUTA'TION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition.
scriptures: I and my Father are one.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.
corruption_summary: Debrecen's bishop, who gave Hungary its Reformed order and fought the antitrinitarians.
corruption_paragraphs: The error Melius faced in Transylvania is the one that always follows a successful appeal to Scripture against tradition: having set aside the councils, a man asks why he should keep the creed they wrote, and concludes that the Trinity is a Greek addition. Francis David made precisely that argument, and he made it as a Reformer.

The principle to recover is that the Trinity is not an inference from councils but the plain speech of Scripture. The commission names the three in one name (Mat 28:19), the apostolic benediction names all three (2Co 13:14), and the Son says outright, “I and my Father are one” (Joh 10:30). A church that cannot say this has not simplified its faith; it has lost its object of worship.

pos: n. (Gaspar Karoli, c. 1529–1591, pastor at Gonc, translator of the first complete Hungarian Bible)
etymology: Persian through Greek Gaspar, treasure-bearer; Karoli, of Nagykaroly, his birthplace.
biblical_def: Gaspar Karoli was pastor of Gonc and senior of the Reformed churches of the Kassa valley, and the chief translator of the first complete Bible in Hungarian. Trained at Wittenberg and Strasbourg, he had already written against the antitrinitarians and on the sufferings of the Hungarian nation under the Turk when, in his late fifties, he gathered a company of scholars and set about the whole of Scripture from Hebrew and Greek. The work was finished in 1590 and printed at Vizsoly under the protection of the Rakoczi family; eight hundred copies were produced, and Karoli died the next year. His version, repeatedly revised but never replaced, is the Hungarian Bible — the book of family worship under Habsburg persecution, in the Reformed colleges, and among the Magyar churches of Transylvania to this day. He wrote in his preface that he had laboured so that his countrymen might read in their own tongue; the apostolic rule is the warrant. “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a translator as one who renders into another language, and a pastor as a minister of the gospel who has the care of a church.
webster_full: TRANSLA'TOR, n. One who renders anything from one language into another.
PAS'TOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
PREF'ACE, n. Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book.

corruption_summary: The pastor of Gonc who gave the Magyars their Bible, printed at Vizsoly in 1590.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Karoli does stand against the assumption that a national Bible is a cultural artefact first and a sacred text second — studied for what it did to a language rather than received for what it says. He translated for readers, not for literature, and the Hungarian prose he created was a by-product.

The principle to recover is that the word is given to be understood and to dwell in a people: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16). The translator's own prayer must be the psalmist's — “Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law” (Psa 119:18) — before his readers can pray it.

pos: n. (the Vizsoly Bible, 1590, the first complete Hungarian Bible, printed at Vizsoly in Zemplen)
etymology: Vizsoly, the village in north-eastern Hungary where the press stood; Greek biblia, books.
biblical_def: The Vizsoly Bible is the first complete Bible in Hungarian, translated chiefly by Gaspar Karoli with a team of fellow pastors and printed at Vizsoly in the county of Zemplen between February 1589 and July 1590. The press was set up for the purpose in a village of a few hundred souls, under the protection of Sigismund Rakoczi, and worked by Balint Mantskovit; about eight hundred copies were printed in two folio volumes, of which some fifty survive. It came to a church already confessionally settled under Melius but without the whole of Scripture in its own tongue, and it arrived just before the Counter-Reformation closed in: for the next two centuries Hungarian Reformed families held worship around this book while their colleges were suppressed and their pastors sent to the galleys. Revised by Albert Molnar in 1608 and many times since, it remains the Hungarian Authorized Version. “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11) describes exactly what the Magyar households did with it, there being for long stretches nowhere else to keep it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the Bible as the volume which contains the Scriptures, and a folio as a book of the largest size, formed by once doubling a sheet.
webster_full: BI'BLE, n. The Book by way of eminence; the sacred volume.
FO'LIO, n. A book of the largest size, formed by once doubling a sheet of paper.
PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed; a printing machine.

corruption_summary: The first complete Hungarian Bible, eight hundred copies from a village press in 1590.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It is worth noticing what the Vizsoly Bible cost and what it bought. A village press, a patron's protection, two years, eight hundred copies — and with that a church survived two centuries of suppression with no seminary, often no pastor, and no legal standing.

The principle to recover is that faith comes by hearing the word and nothing else will serve as a substitute: “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). Where preaching was forbidden, the household reading of this book was the hearing; and a child so taught “hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation” (2Ti 3:15).

pos: n. (Albert Molnar of Szenc, 1574–1634, Hungarian philologist, psalmist and translator)
etymology: Old German Adalbert, noble-bright; Hungarian molnar, a miller.
biblical_def: Albert Molnar of Szenc was the most learned Hungarian of his generation and spent most of his life abroad, at Wittenberg, Heidelberg, Strasbourg, Altdorf, Marburg and Oppenheim, supported by patrons and by his own pen. He gave his church four things it could not have done without. He revised and reissued Karoli's Bible in 1608 at Hanau and again in 1612 at Oppenheim, correcting the text and making it portable. He produced the first scientific Latin–Hungarian dictionary and the first systematic Hungarian grammar, which fixed the written language. He translated the Heidelberg Catechism and Calvin's Institutes into Hungarian, the latter in 1624 — the first full translation into any vernacular of eastern Europe. And in 1607 he published a metrical psalter in Hungarian, versified from the French Genevan psalms of Marot and Beza to the Genevan tunes, which became the hymn-book of Magyar Protestantism and is still sung. “sing ye praises with understanding” (Psa 47:7) was the aim of that last labour, and his grammar and dictionary served the same end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalter as the book of Psalms, and philology as the study of language, its grammar and etymology.
webster_full: PSAL'TER, n. The book of Psalms; a book containing the Psalms separately printed.
PHILOL'OGY, n. Primarily, a love of words; that branch of literature which comprehends grammar and etymology.
MET'RICAL, a. Pertaining to measure; consisting of verses.

corruption_summary: Hungary's philologist, who gave it a psalter, a grammar, a dictionary and the Institutes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Molnar is a standing answer to the notion that scholarship and congregational life belong to different departments. The man who wrote the grammar also wrote the psalter, and for the same reason: a people cannot sing with understanding in a tongue that has not been given a settled form.

The principle to recover is that praise is to be intelligent as well as hearty: “sing ye praises with understanding” (Psa 47:7), “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16). His Genevan tunes carried doctrine into Magyar villages that had no preacher left.

pos: n. (the Confession of Debrecen, 1562, the first Hungarian Reformed confession of faith)
etymology: Debrecen, the Hungarian city on the great plain; Latin confessio, an acknowledging.
biblical_def: The Debrecen Confession, drawn up in 1562 by Peter Melius with Gregory Szegedi and adopted by the synod at Tarcal and Torda, was the first confession of faith of the Hungarian Reformed churches. It is sometimes called the Confessio Catholica, and it was written for two audiences at once: to show the Catholic authorities and the Turkish overlords what the Hungarian Protestants actually taught, and to separate the Reformed from the Lutherans on the supper and from the rising antitrinitarian party on the person of Christ. It is long, closely argued from Scripture and the fathers, and unusually explicit on the Trinity, because that was where the Transylvanian breach was about to open. Within a decade the Hungarian churches moved to the broader and better-ordered Second Helvetic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism, which they still hold, so Debrecen is not now a subordinate standard; but it is the document by which they first took a confessional stand, and it decided which side of the sixteenth century they would be on. “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as a formulary of religious belief, and a synod as a council of ecclesiastics.
webster_full: CONFES'SION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a creed.
SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
ARTICLE, n. A single clause or term; a distinct part of a writing or confession.

Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.

corruption_summary: Hungary's first Reformed confession, 1562, explicit on the Trinity before the breach.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Debrecen Confession illustrates something about the life of confessions that is often misunderstood: a church may draw one up, use it for a generation, and then adopt a better one without any disloyalty. What it may not do is decline to have one, for then it cannot say where it stands when the question is forced.

The principle to recover is that a confession exists to let the church contend and to let it examine. The elder must be able “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9), and the saints must “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3). In 1562 Hungary put the Trinity in writing; in 1566 it was glad it had.

pos: n. (the Consensus of Sandomierz, 1570, the agreement of the Polish Reformed, Lutheran and Bohemian Brethren churches)
etymology: Latin consensus, agreement, a feeling together; Sandomierz, the Polish town on the Vistula.
biblical_def: The Consensus of Sandomierz was signed in April 1570 by the three Protestant bodies of the Polish crown — the Reformed, the Lutherans, and the Bohemian Brethren settled in Great Poland — as a mutual recognition of one another's churches, ministries and sacraments. They did not merge and did not adopt a common confession; each kept its own, and the agreement declared that their differences, chiefly on the manner of Christ's presence in the supper, were not such as to divide the churches. It was the first ecumenical act of its kind in Europe to hold together for any length of time, and it had a political purpose as well: united, the three could and did obtain the Warsaw Confederation of 1573, which guaranteed religious peace to the Polish nobility and made Poland for a generation the most tolerant state in Christendom. Its weakness was that it could not include the antitrinitarian Polish Brethren, who were expressly excluded, nor restrain the Counter-Reformation that reclaimed Poland within a century. “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — Sandomierz asked how much agreement that requires.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines consensus by its root, consent, as agreement of minds in opinion; and union as the junction of two or more things.
webster_full: CONSENT', n. Agreement of the mind to what is proposed or stated by another; accord.
U'NION, n. The act of joining two or more things; concord; agreement.
TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.

Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

corruption_summary: The 1570 Polish agreement of Reformed, Lutherans and Brethren, which bought the peace of 1573.
corruption_paragraphs: Sandomierz is now cited as a precedent for the modern ecumenical project, which is a misuse of it. The three Polish bodies all held the Scriptures to be the only rule, all confessed the Trinity and justification by faith, and all excluded the antitrinitarians by name. The agreement was between churches already agreed on the foundation and differing on one article.

The principle to recover is that the unity commanded is a unity in the truth: “That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee” (Joh 17:21) is a unity patterned on the Trinity itself, which is why those who denied the Trinity could not be party to it. The endeavour is real — “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) — but it has a floor.

pos: n. (John Duncan, 1796–1870, Hebraist, missionary to the Jews at Pest, professor in the Free Church New College)
etymology: Hebrew rabbi, my master, a teacher; Gaelic Donnchadh, brown warrior.
biblical_def: Rabbi Duncan was the nickname Edinburgh gave to John Duncan, and it stuck because it fitted. Born at Aberdeen, for a time a convinced atheist, he was converted under the ministry of Cesar Malan and became perhaps the greatest Hebraist in Scotland and a master of a dozen languages. He went out in 1841 as the Church of Scotland's first missionary to the Jews at Pest in Hungary, where under his ministry Alfred Edersheim, Adolph Saphir and others were converted — a mission that bore more fruit per year than any other of the century. From 1843 he was professor of Hebrew and Oriental languages in the Free Church's New College, where he was hopeless as a lecturer and unforgettable as a man: his students wrote down his table talk, published as Colloquia Peripatetica, and it is for those sayings that he is chiefly read. He was a Calvinist who could say that he was first a Christian, next a catholic, then a Calvinist, fourth a paedobaptist and fifth a Presbyterian. “Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved” (Rom 10:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rabbi as a title of respect given by the Jews to their doctors and teachers, and a Hebraist as one versed in the Hebrew language.
webster_full: RAB'BI, n. A title assumed by the Jewish doctors, signifying master or lord.
HE'BRAIST, n. One versed in the Hebrew language.
COLLO'QUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more.
scriptures: Rom 10:1
Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved.
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
corruption_summary: Scotland's great Hebraist, missionary at Pest and sayer of unforgettable things.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Duncan's ordering of his own identity — Christian first, catholic next, Calvinist third — is a rebuke to a habit found in every confessional tradition, including his own and ours: the habit of leading with the narrowest term, as though the system rather than the Saviour were the thing held.

The principle to recover is the one that sent him to Pest. The gospel is “the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Rom 1:16), and Paul's heart's desire for Israel (Rom 10:1) is not a relic of the apostolic age. Duncan's own confession, when pressed, was Thomas's: “My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28).

pos: n. (John Macdonald, 1779–1849, minister of Ferintosh, called the Apostle of the North)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Gaelic Mac Dhomhnaill, son of Donald; Ferintosh, the chieftain's land.
biblical_def: John Macdonald of Ferintosh was the son of a Reay catechist, a Gaelic preacher of extraordinary power, and the best-known Highland minister of his century, universally called the Apostle of the North. Settled at Ferintosh in the Black Isle from 1813, he preached there and travelled constantly: through Caithness and Sutherland, to Skye and Lewis, and four times to St Kilda, where his visits produced a lasting change in the island's religion. His open-air communion seasons drew crowds in the thousands — at Ferintosh, by some accounts, ten thousand sat on the brae — and he commonly preached five or six times in a day in Gaelic and English. He was deeply read in the Puritans, severe with himself, and plain about the terrors and the consolations alike. He left the establishment at the Disruption of 1843 with his whole congregation and spent his last years building the Free Church in the north. His life was spent in one errand: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15), which for him meant every glen and island within reach of a horse or a boat.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an apostle as one sent, a messenger, and itinerant as travelling, not settled in one place.
webster_full: APOS'TLE, n. A person deputed to execute some important business; a messenger.
ITIN'ERANT, a. Passing or travelling about the country; not settled.
GAEL'IC, a. Pertaining to the Gaels, the Celtic inhabitants of the Highlands of Scotland.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
corruption_summary: The Apostle of the North, Gaelic preacher of the Highland communion seasons.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Highland communion season which Macdonald served is widely misremembered as a festival of gloom, a week of fencing the tables to keep people away. The records say otherwise: the preparation was searching, and the Monday was thanksgiving, and the crowds walked days to be there.

The principle to recover is the errand itself, unbounded by parish lines: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15). The anointing Isaiah describes is “to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted” (Isa 61:1), and a man who means to finish his course with joy (Act 20:24) will go where the hearers are.

pos: n. (Lachlan Mackenzie, 1754–1819, minister of Lochcarron, known as Mr Lachlan)
etymology: Gaelic Lachlann, from the Norse for a man of the lochs; Mac Coinnich, son of the fair one.
biblical_def: Lachlan Mackenzie of Lochcarron, known throughout the Highlands simply as Mr Lachlan, was minister of that Wester Ross parish from 1782 until his death in 1819, and is remembered as the most spiritually penetrating of the Highland fathers. He was a sickly man who walked with difficulty and was often unable to leave his house, and his parish was poor and remote; yet his sermons, taken down by hearers and printed long afterwards, show an unusual gift for the anatomy of a believer's heart, and his sayings circulated through the north for a century. He was reputed to have a measure of foresight in particular cases, which the Highland tradition treasured and which he himself treated with reserve. His theology was experimental Calvinism of the strictest kind, and his constant theme was the believer's emptiness and Christ's fulness. “I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing” (Joh 15:5) was the burden of his preaching, and his own long weakness was the commentary on it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infirmity as an unsound state of the body, a failing, and experimental as known by experience.
webster_full: INFIRM'ITY, n. An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; feebleness.
EXPERIMENT'AL, a. Known by experiment or experience; derived from experience.
FUL'NESS, n. The state of being filled, so as to leave no part vacant; abundance.
scriptures: Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
Php 1:21
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
corruption_summary: Mr Lachlan of Lochcarron, the Highland anatomist of the believer's heart.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Experimental preaching of Mackenzie's kind is, however, widely suspected now on two grounds at once: that it breeds introspection, and that it makes assurance hang on feelings. His sermons answer both. He examined the heart in order to drive it out of itself, and every diagnosis ends at Christ's fulness rather than at the hearer's state.

The principle to recover is the arithmetic of the vine: “without me ye can do nothing” (Joh 15:5), and therefore “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:9). A bedridden minister in a poor parish is not thereby a diminished one, and his portion is the psalmist's — “Whom have I in heaven but thee?” (Psa 73:25).
